{
  "claims": [
    {
      "cause": "Tightening monetary policy from a loose starting stance versus from a tight starting stance",
      "effect": "Different magnitudes of impact on inflation (smaller when tightening from a loose stance; larger when tightening from a tight stance)",
      "linking_explanation": "The transmission of monetary policy to inflation is subject to threshold non-linearities; the elasticity of inflation to policy tightening depends on the initial stance, with weaker effects when conditions are already loose and stronger effects when conditions are tight.",
      "document_reference": "Batch 3, paragraph 1 (citing Calza and Sousa, 2005)",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "“research also finds … depends on thresholds”",
      "modulator_temporal": "NA"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Falling policy rates and quantitative easing (QE)",
      "effect": "Decline in reference (OIS) rates",
      "linking_explanation": "Policy rate cuts lower expected short rates and QE depresses term premia, both reducing risk-free reference rates across maturities.",
      "document_reference": "Batch 3, paragraph 2",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "NA"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Decline in reference (OIS) rates",
      "effect": "Widening of mortgage spreads",
      "linking_explanation": "Mortgage rates did not fall proportionately or quickly as reference rates fell, increasing the gap between mortgage rates and maturity-matched OIS rates.",
      "document_reference": "Batch 3, paragraph 2",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "Over the next decade after the GFC, mortgage rates fell only very slowly"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Changes in policy/reference (risk-free) rates",
      "effect": "Changes in household mortgage rates occur with a lag",
      "linking_explanation": "Observed co-movement weakened after the GFC and mortgage rates adjusted slowly to shifts in reference rates, indicating lagged pass-through from policy/reference rates to mortgage pricing faced by households.",
      "document_reference": "Batch 3, paragraph 2",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "“This is evidence, at least over the sample period we are looking at, of lagged pass-through”",
      "modulator_temporal": "NA"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Global Financial Crisis (GFC)",
      "effect": "Breakdown of the close co-movement between mortgage rates and reference (OIS) rates",
      "linking_explanation": "During the financial crisis, the previously tight linkage between mortgage and reference rates ceased to hold, altering the transmission from policy/reference rates to mortgage pricing.",
      "document_reference": "Batch 3, paragraph 2",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "Since the GFC period"
    },
    {
      "cause": "UK ‘mini-budget’ market turmoil (September 2022)",
      "effect": "Spike in interest rates, with reference rates spiking before mortgage rates",
      "linking_explanation": "Market stress raised reference rates sharply; mortgage rates rose with a delay due to slower pass-through to retail pricing.",
      "document_reference": "Batch 3, paragraph 3",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "“spike around the mini-budget turmoil” (association implied rather than quantified)",
      "modulator_temporal": "September 2022 and subsequent retracement period"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Rising risk-free/reference rates",
      "effect": "More rapid transmission to higher mortgage rates",
      "linking_explanation": "Pass-through from reference rates to mortgage rates is state-dependent, operating more quickly when rates are rising.",
      "document_reference": "Batch 3, paragraph 3",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "“It appears … suggesting more rapid transmission as interest rates rise”",
      "modulator_temporal": "NA"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Falling risk-free/reference rates",
      "effect": "Slower transmission to lower mortgage rates",
      "linking_explanation": "State-dependent pass-through implies that mortgage rates adjust downwards more slowly than reference rates when rates are falling.",
      "document_reference": "Batch 3, paragraph 3",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "“It appears … suggesting … slower transmission as interest rates fall”",
      "modulator_temporal": "NA"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Increases in Bank Rate (tightening cycle)",
      "effect": "Mortgage rates initially rose closely in line with reference rates",
      "linking_explanation": "During the early phase of the tightening cycle, the pass-through from reference rates to mortgage rates was relatively close, before later divergences due to lags and state dependence.",
      "document_reference": "Batch 3, paragraph 3",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "“tracked reference rates quite closely, initially”",
      "modulator_temporal": "Initial phase after Bank Rate increases"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Monetary policy tightening by the MPC over the last twelve months",
      "effect": "Considerable downward effect on equity prices",
      "linking_explanation": "Higher discount rates and tighter financial conditions reduce the present value of expected future cash flows, depressing equity valuations.",
      "document_reference": "Batch 3, paragraph 4",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "Over the last twelve months"
    }
  ]
}

{
  "claims": [
    {
      "cause": "A 100 basis point monetary policy (tightening) shock",
      "effect": "A persistent increase in the 1-year nominal interest rate",
      "linking_explanation": "A contractionary monetary policy shock lifts current and expected short rates, which feeds into the 1-year yield and keeps it elevated for a period.",
      "document_reference": "Page 14, Chart 7 description (top-left panel)",
      "quantifications": "Shock size: 100 bps; duration of effect: around 12 months",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "Effect lasts around twelve months after the shock"
    },
    {
      "cause": "A monetary policy tightening shock in the UK (with only the home central bank tightening)",
      "effect": "An appreciation of the Sterling exchange rate index",
      "linking_explanation": "Higher UK interest rates relative to abroad raise the return on Sterling assets; via interest rate differentials (UIP), capital inflows appreciate the currency.",
      "document_reference": "Page 14, Chart 7 description (top-right panel)",
      "quantifications": "Peak exchange-rate effect occurs 2–3 months after the shock",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "Peak effect at two to three months following the shock"
    },
    {
      "cause": "A contractionary monetary policy shock",
      "effect": "A delayed decline in the level of real GDP",
      "linking_explanation": "Monetary tightening raises borrowing costs and tightens financial conditions, reducing demand with a lag; the response is consistent with monetary policy lags and the notion (in the cited framing) that GDP responds after inflation.",
      "document_reference": "Page 14, discussion of real GDP response",
      "quantifications": "Real GDP peak response: approximately -1.25% after around two years; lags consistent with 18–24 months",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "Described as statistically significant",
      "modulator_temporal": "Barely moves on impact; gradually falls; peak effect around two years after the shock"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Contractionary monetary policy",
      "effect": "A permanently negative effect on the level of output relative to trend (with subsequent recovery in growth rates)",
      "linking_explanation": "The level of output shifts downward relative to trend following tightening; although growth resumes, the level remains lower, indicating a persistent level effect of the shock.",
      "document_reference": "Page 14, sentence beginning 'The results also suggest a permanently negative effect...'",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "Uses the phrasing 'suggest' indicating some tentativeness",
      "modulator_temporal": "Characterized as 'permanently' negative in level relative to trend"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Monetary policy tightening",
      "effect": "An instantaneous, statistically significant decline in the level of CPI",
      "linking_explanation": "A fast exchange-rate pass-through mechanism: the monetary tightening induces an immediate Sterling appreciation, reducing import prices and quickly lowering the CPI level.",
      "document_reference": "Page 14, Chart 7 description (bottom-right panel)",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "The reliance on the exchange-rate channel is stated as 'likely'",
      "modulator_temporal": "Instantaneous effect on CPI in the model"
    },
    {
      "cause": "A sequence of monetary policy shocks occurring in close succession",
      "effect": "Overlapping effects that operate before the full effect of any single shock is realized",
      "linking_explanation": "New shocks arrive while earlier shocks are still propagating through the economy’s lags, layering the transmission and altering the realized dynamics of macro responses.",
      "document_reference": "Page 14, sentence beginning 'In reality, the economy has faced a sequence of these shocks...'",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "Described as occurring 'in the past year' and 'before we have seen the full effect'"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Tightening by other (foreign) central banks",
      "effect": "Changes in UK financial conditions, including via the exchange rate, that interact with the transmission of UK monetary policy",
      "linking_explanation": "Foreign tightening affects interest differentials and global financial conditions, influencing Sterling and the overall stance facing the UK, thereby modulating the domestic transmission channel.",
      "document_reference": "Page 14, sentences 'And, other central banks have also been tightening policy.' and prior reference to the exchange rate’s role in financial conditions",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "NA"
    },
    {
      "cause": "A period of surging and persistently high inflation (relative to the low and stable inflation estimation period)",
      "effect": "Potential alteration of the monetary policy transmission mechanism",
      "linking_explanation": "High inflation may change expectations formation and price-setting behavior, potentially modifying the speed and strength of transmission compared with low-inflation regimes.",
      "document_reference": "Pages 14–15, questions 'Might these results be affected... Could high inflation itself affect the monetary transmission mechanism?'",
      "quantifications": "Reference period: 'the last 18 months' of high inflation",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "Expressed as questions ('Might', 'Could'), indicating uncertainty",
      "modulator_temporal": "Pertains to the recent 18-month high-inflation period"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Announced changes in the monetary policy rate (especially rate hikes)",
      "effect": "Firms revise their price expectations downward and reduce uncertainty around those expectations",
      "linking_explanation": "A direct expectations channel: policy announcements provide information or signals that lead firms to adjust their beliefs about future prices and the dispersion of those beliefs.",
      "document_reference": "Page 15, reference to Di Pace et al. (2023) and accompanying text",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "Described as 'some evidence'",
      "modulator_temporal": "Adjustments occur upon announcement; pertains to 'within the period of the shock'"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Monetary policy operating through the direct expectations channel",
      "effect": "Price-setting behavior is affected within the period of the shock",
      "linking_explanation": "As firms’ price expectations fall following a rate hike, they adjust price-setting more quickly, bringing forward the impact of policy on inflation.",
      "document_reference": "Page 15, sentence '...show some evidence for a direct expectations channel of monetary policy which could affect price setting already within the period of the shock.'",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "Phrased as 'could', indicating uncertainty",
      "modulator_temporal": "Within the same period as the policy shock"
    },
    {
      "cause": "A higher share of backward-looking price-setters in the economy (expectations formation assumption)",
      "effect": "Alteration of the monetary policy transmission mechanism",
      "linking_explanation": "When a greater share of firms set prices based on past inflation (backward-looking), the dynamics of inflation and output in response to policy change, modifying the speed and pattern of transmission.",
      "document_reference": "Page 15, Section 5 introduction describing the toy model varying the share of backward-looking price-setters",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "The model is described as a 'toy model' that 'disregards many other features of the real world'",
      "modulator_temporal": "NA"
    }
  ]
}

{
  "claims": [
    {
      "cause": "Higher degree of backward-looking inflation expectations among firms/agents",
      "effect": "Greater inflation persistence following a given shock",
      "linking_explanation": "When price-setters base expectations on past inflation rather than future fundamentals, shocks are propagated through inertia, slowing reversion of inflation to target even when the underlying shock is unchanged.",
      "document_reference": "Bank of England Page 16 (paragraph beginning 'In this model, I find ...')",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "NA"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Expectations formation is mainly backward-looking",
      "effect": "A given monetary tightening has less effect on reducing inflation",
      "linking_explanation": "Backward-looking expectations detach inflation dynamics from current demand and supply conditions; since monetary policy primarily influences demand, the transmission from policy tightening to inflation is weakened.",
      "document_reference": "Bank of England Page 16 (sentence: 'A given monetary tightening has less of an effect on inflation if expectations formation is mainly backward-looking...')",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "NA"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Expectations formation is mainly backward-looking",
      "effect": "Worsened inflation-activity trade-off in the face of a shock",
      "linking_explanation": "With weaker monetary-policy transmission to inflation, larger output costs are required to disinflate, deteriorating the trade-off between stabilizing inflation and stabilizing activity.",
      "document_reference": "Bank of England Page 16 (sentence: '...which thereby worsens any inflation-activity trade-off in the face of a shock.')",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "NA"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Energy price surges",
      "effect": "Higher share of backward-looking agents in the UK",
      "linking_explanation": "Empirical research indicates the composition of expectation rules shifts toward backward-looking behavior when energy prices surge, implying external price shocks influence expectation formation.",
      "document_reference": "Bank of England Page 16 (reference to Cornea-Madeira and Madeira, 2022)",
      "quantifications": "Share of backward/forward-looking agents has fluctuated between 20% and 80% over most of the last 50 years, with a median around 50% (context given in footnote 12).",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "For most of the last 50 years"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Inflationary cost-push shock",
      "effect": "Prices increase above levels implied by domestic demand conditions",
      "linking_explanation": "An exogenous rise in firms’ costs shifts pricing upward independent of domestic demand, akin to global goods or energy price shocks.",
      "document_reference": "Bank of England Page 16 (paragraph beginning 'Returning to the model, we can trace out ... a so-called cost-push shock...')",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "NA"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Cost-push shock in an economy with fully forward-looking, model-consistent expectations and a central bank using a balanced Taylor rule",
      "effect": "Limited and short-lived impacts on activity and prices; output gap quickly returns to zero and inflation reverts toward target",
      "linking_explanation": "Forward-looking firms anticipate future conditions and policy; the Taylor-rule response stabilizes the output gap and price level, curtailing the shock’s effects.",
      "document_reference": "Bank of England Page 16 (Chart 8 description: 'In this economy, the cost-push shock has a very limited and short-lived impact on activity and prices. The output gap jumps on impact but quickly returns to zero... then reverts towards target.')",
      "quantifications": "Inflation peaks after four quarters",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "Short-lived; inflation peaks after four quarters before reverting"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Lagged nature of year-on-year inflation measurement",
      "effect": "Inflation peaks after four quarters following the shock",
      "linking_explanation": "Year-on-year inflation compares to the same quarter in the previous year, so the impact of a shock shows with a lag, generating a delayed peak.",
      "document_reference": "Bank of England Page 16 (sentence: 'Because of the lagged nature of year-on-year inflation ... it peaks after four quarters and then reverts towards target.')",
      "quantifications": "Peak after 4 quarters",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "After four quarters"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Introducing a modest degree of backward-looking inflation expectations formation",
      "effect": "Output gap becomes more negative for longer",
      "linking_explanation": "Greater inflation persistence requires tighter or more prolonged policy responses, deepening and extending the negative output gap.",
      "document_reference": "Bank of England Page 16 (paragraph beginning 'The behaviours of the output gap and inflation change dramatically when we introduce a modest degree of backward-looking...')",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "For longer"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Introducing a modest degree of backward-looking inflation expectations formation",
      "effect": "Inflation peaks higher and remains above target for an extended period",
      "linking_explanation": "Backward-looking pricing feeds past inflation into current pricing, amplifying the peak and prolonging deviations from target.",
      "document_reference": "Bank of England Page 16 (same paragraph as above)",
      "quantifications": "NA",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "Extended period of time"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Further increasing the share of backward-looking agents (from 40% to 80% in the model calibration)",
      "effect": "Output and inflation become strongly hump-shaped and remain away from equilibrium for the entire plotted period",
      "linking_explanation": "Higher backward-lookingness intensifies intrinsic persistence and amplifies the propagation of shocks, producing pronounced hump-shaped dynamics and prolonged disequilibrium.",
      "document_reference": "Bank of England Page 16–17 (paragraphs describing Chart 8 and persistence; footnote 12 on shares)",
      "quantifications": "Model lines use 0%, 40%, and 80% backward-looking firms; away from equilibrium for 4 years (entire plotted period).",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "Entire plotted period (4 years)"
    },
    {
      "cause": "Increasing the share of backward-looking firms by equal increments",
      "effect": "Disproportionately larger changes in inflation and output behavior (non-linear response)",
      "linking_explanation": "Changes in expectations formation introduce non-linearities so that equal increases in backward-lookingness yield increasingly stark macroeconomic responses.",
      "document_reference": "Bank of England Page 17 (paragraph beginning 'These pictures also reveal an important non-linearity...')",
      "quantifications": "Equal increments illustrated at 0%, 40%, 80% backward-looking firms",
      "modulator_uncertainty": "NA",
      "modulator_temporal": "NA"
    }
  ]
}
